html:
The most common side effects of retatrutide in Eli Lilly’s TRIUMPH trials were stomach and gut effects: nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, vomiting and reduced appetite. The trials also reported dysesthesia, an abnormal or burning skin sensation, more often than with placebo. Most events were mild to moderate, and more people stopped retatrutide because of side effects than stopped placebo.

These figures come from phase 3 trials reported between December 2025 and October 2026. Retatrutide is not yet approved as a medicine, so there is no official label listing its side effects. Below, we go through what each trial reported, why these effects happen, and what is still unknown.

What are the most common side effects of retatrutide?

Across the TRIUMPH trials, the side effects of retatrutide fall into three groups: stomach and gut effects, abnormal skin sensations, and changes in blood pressure and heart rate. The first group is by far the most common.

Nausea, diarrhoea and other stomach effects

Stomach and gut effects were the most frequent side effects in every trial. In TRIUMPH-1, the largest obesity trial, nausea affected 28.6% to 42.4% of people on retatrutide, versus 14.8% on placebo, and diarrhoea affected 25.2% to 34.1%, versus 13.5%. Constipation (23.8% to 26.1%, versus 10.9%) and vomiting (10.6% to 25.3%, versus 4.8%) were also more common than with placebo.

Rates rose with the dose. Reduced appetite was also common: in TRIUMPH-2 it affected 5.8% to 17.1% of people on retatrutide, versus 4.5% on placebo. Lilly described these effects as generally mild to moderate, with most resolving during treatment. This pattern is familiar from the drugs in the same family, semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Dysesthesia: abnormal skin sensations

Dysesthesia is the side effect that sets retatrutide apart. Lilly defines it in these trials as a burning skin sensation and related events. It was not reported in the phase 2 trial, then appeared in every phase 3 obesity trial, always more often than with placebo. Rates ranged from 4.5% in TRIUMPH-2 to 20.9% in TRIUMPH-4, against 1.3% or less on placebo; the table below gives the figures for each trial.

Lilly’s medical information team says these events were mostly mild to moderate. In TRIUMPH-4, Lilly said dysesthesia did not appear to lead people to stop treatment.

Low blood pressure and heart rate changes

The full TRIUMPH-1 results, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in September 2026, reported symptoms of low blood pressure. They were dose-dependent and more common in people also taking blood pressure medicines. In the earlier phase 2 trial, heart rate rose with the dose for up to 24 weeks and then declined.

Retatrutide side effects in each TRIUMPH trial

The four TRIUMPH obesity trials tested retatrutide in different groups of people, and the side-effect rates differ between them. Each range below runs from the lowest to the highest dose tested, compared with placebo.

Trial (reported) Who took part Most common side effects Dysesthesia Stopped because of side effects
TRIUMPH-2 (July 2026) Adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight Diarrhoea 27.4% to 33.6% vs 13.2%; nausea 13.7% to 28.0% vs 8.0% 4.5% to 7.3% vs 0.7% 3.8% to 11.6% vs 4.9%
TRIUMPH-3 (July 2026) Adults with severe obesity and established heart disease Diarrhoea 24.4% to 30.1% vs 8.7%; nausea 21.7% to 22.4% vs 5.8% 6.4% vs 1.3% 9.8% to 13.5% vs 4.8%
TRIUMPH-1 (May 2026) Adults with obesity or overweight and a related condition, without diabetes Nausea 28.6% to 42.4% vs 14.8%; diarrhoea 25.2% to 34.1% vs 13.5% 5.1% to 12.5% vs 0.9% 4.1% to 11.3% vs 4.9%
TRIUMPH-4 (December 2025) Adults with obesity or overweight and knee osteoarthritis Nausea 43%, diarrhoea 33% and vomiting 21% on the highest dose 8.8% to 20.9% vs 0.7% 12.2% to 18.2% vs about 4%

Two patterns stand out. Stomach and gut effects were the most common side effect in every trial, and dysesthesia was highest in TRIUMPH-4. Most figures are company-reported topline results; full TRIUMPH-1 results were published in the New England Journal of Medicine in September 2026.

How many people stopped retatrutide because of side effects?

In the phase 3 trials, between about 4% and 18% of people on retatrutide stopped treatment because of side effects, depending on the trial and the dose. On placebo, the figure was around 4% to 5%. The gap was generally small at the lowest dose and wider at higher doses.

Why some people stopped

Lilly has not yet published a full breakdown of why people stopped. Stomach and gut effects were the most common side effects overall. In TRIUMPH-4, Lilly also attributed some stops to perceived excessive weight loss: some participants felt they were losing weight faster or further than they wanted.

Who was more likely to stop

Body weight at the start seems to matter. In TRIUMPH-4, stopping rates were lower among people with a higher starting BMI. When Lilly excluded participants with a BMI below 35, the rates fell to 8.8% and 12.1% on the two retatrutide doses, versus 4.8% on placebo. Analysts at BMO Capital Markets read this as a sign that the speed and strength of weight loss was too much for some people with a lower BMI.

For comparison, the phase 2 trial published in 2023 reported that 6% to 16% of people on retatrutide stopped because of side effects, versus none on placebo. Starting at a lower dose partly reduced stomach side effects in that trial.

Why does retatrutide cause these side effects?

Most of retatrutide’s side effects follow from what it is designed to do. It is a GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist, research code LY3437943, so one molecule acts on three hormone receptors at once.

How the GLP-1 action slows digestion

The GLP-1 part slows how fast the stomach empties and acts on appetite centres in the brain. That is what reduces hunger, and it is also what causes nausea, fullness, vomiting and changes in bowel habits. If you want the full picture of the three receptors, we explain how retatrutide works in our longer guide.

Why the skin sensations are not yet explained

The cause of dysesthesia with retatrutide is not yet clear. Lilly has reported how often it happens and how severe it is, but has not published an explanation of why. It was not seen in the phase 2 trial, which is one reason analysts flagged it as a new signal when TRIUMPH-4 reported in December 2025.

How rapid weight loss affects blood pressure

Rapid weight loss can lower blood pressure, which may explain why low blood pressure symptoms were more common in people already taking blood pressure medicines. A rise in heart rate has also been seen with other drugs that act on the GLP-1 receptor.

What is still unknown about retatrutide’s safety?

The TRIUMPH trials answer a lot, but four questions are still open.

Long-term safety

The phase 3 obesity trials ran for 68 to 80 weeks. That is long enough to see common side effects, but not rare ones or effects that take years to appear. Lilly is running a separate trial, TRIUMPH-Outcomes, to study heart and kidney outcomes in adults with obesity over a longer period.

Heart safety

Early signals are reassuring but not conclusive. In TRIUMPH-3, which enrolled people with established heart disease, major cardiovascular events happened less often than expected in both the retatrutide and placebo groups. Lilly noted that the trial was not designed to show a statistically significant difference, so it cannot yet prove retatrutide protects the heart.

Dysesthesia over time

We know how often dysesthesia happened and that it was mostly mild to moderate. What has not been published in detail is when it starts, how long it lasts, and whether it fully resolves after stopping.

Why there is no official label yet

A drug’s official side-effect list, warnings and contraindications come from its approved label. Retatrutide does not have one, because no regulator has approved it yet. Lilly plans to file with the US Food and Drug Administration in the first quarter of 2027, and the label would be written during that review.

Is retatrutide approved yet?

Not yet. Retatrutide is not approved as a medicine in Indonesia or anywhere else. Lilly says its obesity data package is complete and plans to submit it to the FDA in the first quarter of 2027. BPOM would review it separately for Indonesia.

Until then, retatrutide is available in Bali as a research compound, supplied for laboratory and research use. It is sometimes sold as “reta”, “Triple G”, “GLP-3 RT” or “GLP-3 RTA”. The “GLP-3” label is misleading, since there is no GLP-3 hormone; the “3” refers to the three receptors retatrutide acts on.

For research buyers, we supply retatrutide in Bali as a research compound. Our retatrutide is sold for research use only. It is not a Lilly product, it is not a BPOM-registered medicine, and it is not approved for human use.

Conclusion

Retatrutide’s side effects in the TRIUMPH trials were mostly stomach and gut effects: nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, vomiting and reduced appetite, generally mild to moderate and more common at higher doses. Dysesthesia, a burning or abnormal skin sensation, is the effect that sets it apart from semaglutide and tirzepatide, reported in every phase 3 obesity trial at rates of roughly 4% to 21%.

Between about 4% and 18% of trial participants stopped retatrutide because of side effects, compared with around 4% to 5% on placebo. Long-term safety, heart outcomes and the course of dysesthesia are still being studied.

Retatrutide is not yet approved as a medicine, and its official label will only exist after regulators review it, starting with Lilly’s planned FDA filing in early 2027. For now, it is available in Bali as a research compound, supplied for research use only.

Frequently asked questions

How long do retatrutide side effects last?

In the TRIUMPH-2 and TRIUMPH-3 trials, Lilly reported that most side effects were mild to moderate and that the majority resolved during treatment.

Is dysesthesia from retatrutide serious?

In the trials, dysesthesia was mostly mild to moderate. In TRIUMPH-4, where it was most common, Lilly said it did not appear to lead people to stop treatment. Its cause and how long it lasts have not been fully reported.

Do retatrutide side effects depend on the dose?

Yes. In the TRIUMPH trials, nausea, vomiting, dysesthesia and stopping because of side effects were generally more common at higher doses.

Are retatrutide side effects worse than tirzepatide’s?

There is no full head-to-head safety comparison published yet. In a type 2 diabetes trial against Mounjaro (TRANSCEND-T2D-1), analysts at RBC Capital Markets said overall tolerability was worse with retatrutide.

Does retatrutide lower blood pressure?

The full TRIUMPH-1 results reported symptoms of low blood pressure. They were dose-dependent and more common in people who were also taking blood pressure medicines.

What does “efek samping retatrutide” mean?

It is Indonesian for “retatrutide side effects”. The answer is the same: mainly nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, vomiting and reduced appetite, plus dysesthesia, as reported in the TRIUMPH trials.
